source.title: An Analysis of the Association Between National Football League Players Association (NFLPA) Ratings and Player Injuries

paper.citation: Davidson R., Gordon S., Hussain A., Schneider S. An Analysis of the Association Between National Football League Players Association (NFLPA) Ratings and Player Injuries. Cureus. 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.110909.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: At the NFL-team level, are NFLPA rankings of training staffs or strength coaches correlated with the number of players missing games or total player-weeks missed because of injury? Participants: No individual participant cohort was analyzed; the unit was all 32 NFL teams, using aggregated public data. Sport and level: Professional American football, 2024–2025 NFL regular season. Design: Cross-sectional ecological correlation study with team-level aggregation (n=32). Exposure or intervention: NFLPA anonymous player-survey rankings for “Training Staff” and “Strength coaches”; lower rank indicated a better rating.
paper.tldr: Across the season, 1,149 players missed a game and 5,811 player-weeks were missed; team means were 36.097 players and 183.645 player-weeks. Pearson correlations were not statistically significant for training-staff rank versus players missing games (r=-.0300, p=.435), strength-staff rank versus players missing games (r=-.2675, p=.063), training-staff rank versus weeks missed (r=-.0310, p=.433), or strength-staff rank versus weeks missed (r=-.2378, p=.089). NFLPA ratings may describe player experience and workplace environment, but these data do not validate them as performance indicators for medical or strength-and-conditioning staffs.
paper.methods: Design: Cross-sectional ecological correlation study with team-level aggregation (n=32). Exposure or intervention: NFLPA anonymous player-survey rankings for “Training Staff” and “Strength coaches”; lower rank indicated a better rating. Comparator: Each staff ranking against (1) players missing at least one game and (2) total player-weeks missed. Measurements and outcomes: Public NFLPA rankings and Pro-Football-Reference injury reports; outcomes were unadjusted team counts and player-weeks, not unique injury events or individual risk. Analysis: Pearson product-moment and Spearman rank correlations, significance threshold p=.05.
paper.findings: Across the season, 1,149 players missed a game and 5,811 player-weeks were missed; team means were 36.097 players and 183.645 player-weeks. Pearson correlations were not statistically significant for training-staff rank versus players missing games (r=-.0300, p=.435), strength-staff rank versus players missing games (r=-.2675, p=.063), training-staff rank versus weeks missed (r=-.0310, p=.433), or strength-staff rank versus weeks missed (r=-.2378, p=.089). Spearman correlations were likewise nonsignificant: ρ=.0344 (p=.574), -.2014 (p=.130), -.0374 (p=.420), and -.2274 (p=.099), respectively. Linear fits explained little variance: R²=.001 for both training-staff comparisons, .072 for strength-coach rank versus players missing games, and .057 for strength-coach rank versus weeks missed.
paper.limitations: Authors emphasized ecological fallacy, uncontrolled confounding (age, experience, playing style, facilities, surfaces, environment), possible illness/suspension miscoding, likability bias, ambiguous “Training Staff” wording, and retrospective selection/recall bias. Additional transfer limitation — interpretation: NFLPA satisfaction ranks and raw NFL team injury counts are not equivalent to objective evaluations of staff practice, program quality, or individual injury risk. Additional causal limitation — interpretation: Null team-level correlations neither show that staff quality has no effect nor identify causes of injury burden.
paper.practicalImplications: NFLPA ratings may describe player experience and workplace environment, but these data do not validate them as performance indicators for medical or strength-and-conditioning staffs. Staff evaluation should use objective process and outcome measures with appropriate exposure adjustment and individual-level longitudinal data; this ecological null result should not drive personnel judgments.

paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, nFLPA ratings may describe player experience and workplace environment, but these data do not validate them as performance indicators for medical or strength-and-conditioning staffs. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
